questions.q: What do we call a material that has a shiny surface when light falls on it?
questions.a: Such a material is called lustrous. A wrong answer like "hard" reveals the student is confusing the property of appearance with the property of texture or resistance to touch.

questions.q: If you can easily press a material with your fingers, how would you describe its hardness?
questions.a: The material is described as soft. If the student says it is "non-lustrous," they are confusing the physical property of hardness with the property of light reflection.

questions.q: You have a glass of water. You add a spoonful of sand to it and stir. Will the sand disappear? Why or why not?
questions.a: The sand will not disappear; it is insoluble. This is because particles of insoluble materials do not mix uniformly into water to become invisible, unlike sugar or salt.

questions.q: Compare a piece of iron and a piece of rubber. Which one is harder, and how do you know?
questions.a: Iron is harder than rubber because it is more difficult to scratch or compress. A student saying they are "equal" fails to understand that hardness is a relative property that can be tested through physical resistance.

questions.q: Your friend wants to make a boat out of paper, but you want to make one out of metal. Which material is more suitable for staying in water for a long time? Justify your answer.
questions.a: The metal boat is more suitable because it is insoluble and holds its form, whereas paper becomes soggy and may disintegrate. A wrong answer suggests the student hasn't considered how solubility and material strength affect object durability.

questions.q: Imagine a new material that is opaque, very hard, and insoluble in water. Suggest one object you could make with it.
questions.a: An example would be a construction brick or a heavy-duty hammer head. A poor answer would be a "drinking straw," which ignores the requirement for hardness or potentially the need for transparency/flexibility.
